title: Can and may
goal: Express ability, permission and possibility with the insert *-ebil*, and inability with *-eme*.
bekal: asking permission and offering help politely

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Okul ofisinde
dialogs.intro: Budi knocks on the door of the school office. Ayşe is sorting files at her desk.

lines.text: Ayşe Hanım, bir şey sorabilir miyim?

lines.text: Salı günü derse gelemeyeceğim. İzin alabilir miyim?

notes: **-ebilmek was originally two verbs fused together**: the main stem + *bilmek* (to know). So "I can come" is literally "I know how to come". English *can* has a similar history: it once meant "to know".

**This insert never stands alone.** After *-ebil* there must always be a tense suffix: *gelebilirim* (can, in general), *gelebiliyorum* (can, right now), *gelebildim* (could, managed to), *gelebileceğim* (will be able to).

**İzin almak means "to take permission", not "to ask for it".** Turkish uses *almak* for many things English says with other verbs: *ders almak* (take a class), *duş almak* (take a shower), *nefes almak* (breathe), *haber almak* (get news).
**Geç kalma!** is a prohibition form, unpacked in unit 15. Literally "don't stay late" — Turkish uses *geç kalmak* for "to be late", not a single word.

blocks.text: To say "can" or "may", insert **-ebil / -abil** between the stem and the tense suffix. If the stem ends in a vowel, a linking *y* goes in.

blocks.title: Three meanings in one form
items: *Yapabilirim* can mean three things, and context tells them apart: **ability** (I'm able to do it), **permission** (I'm allowed to do it), and **possibility** (I might do it).
To ask permission, the first-person question is almost always the one used: *Girebilir miyim?* (may I come in?), *Oturabilir miyim?* (may I sit?), *Bakabilir miyim?* (may I look?).

blocks.text: The negative isn't *-ebilme* but a shorter insert: **-eme / -ama**. The *bil* piece disappears completely.

Can't
English
rows: I won't be able to come

blocks.text: Look at the first row: the aorist negative uses the special pattern from unit 13 — *gelemem*, not *gelemezim*. For *biz*: *gelemeyiz*.

blocks.title: Two negatives, two meanings
items: *Gelmiyorum* = I'm not coming (because I choose not to). *Gelemiyorum* = I CAN'T come (something's in the way).
One letter separates them, and the difference is big. If you're turning down an invitation because you're busy, use the second — it sounds like a reason, not a refusal.

blocks.text: There's a third form that's rarely taught but often used: *-meyebil*, "may not" or "might not". *Gelmeyebilirsin* = you don't have to come. *Yağmur yağmayabilir* = it might not rain.

blocks.title: Words that go with permission
items: *Elbette* and *tabii* both mean "of course" and are interchangeable. *Elbette* is a little firmer; *tabii* (often spelled *tabi*) is more casual.
To decline gently, *maalesef* (unfortunately) almost always goes in front: *Maalesef bugün gelemem.*

blocks.title: Unit 12 review
items: Cover the Turkish and rebuild these from memory: "What are you doing this weekend?" · "We're going to Cappadocia." · "How many days will we stay?" · "I won't come." · "Maybe I'll study."
Then put these into the future: *geliyorum*, *yapıyorsun*, *kalıyoruz*.
